solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: They wallow in shoot-’em-up apps, I suspect

indicators.note: a suspect thing is dubious and not to be taken as it stands, so the letters before it get rearranged

blocks.note: all fourteen letters taken as printed, punctuation ignored

explanation.surface: Someone confesses a suspicion that gamers binge on violent shooting apps.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing 'I' belongs to the fodder, not to a speaker: 'I suspect' reads as one phrase, but only 'suspect' is the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippos famously spend their days lolling in rivers and mud pools, so a description of that habit serves as a playful definition.

clue.text: Revolutionary new doctor dropping Oscar in it

indicators.note: the doctor lets one letter fall away, so the NATO word 'Oscar' is removed from him
the new doctor is placed inside 'it', which wraps around him

blocks.note: taken literally; it becomes the outer shell
O is Oscar in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A news snippet about a radical new medic who has lost an Oscar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' tempts you towards film awards, but it is simply the NATO word for the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurgent is a rebel rising against authority, a synonym for a revolutionary.

clue.text: Pyramid architect in romp on ziggurat

indicators.note: the answer sits in the run of letters of the following words, spanning their word breaks

blocks.note: the end of 'romp', all of 'on' and the start of 'ziggurat'

explanation.surface: An ancient builder frolicking atop a stepped Mesopotamian temple.
explanation.walkthrough: The ziggurat primes you for a real ancient architect, but the pyramid here is a financial fraud: Charles Ponzi gave his name to the Ponzi scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Ponzi devised the fraudulent investment scheme, a kind of pyramid scheme, that still bears his name.

clue.text: Drive to light and extremely pretty country

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outer letters of 'pretty' are kept

explanation.surface: A travel brochure line: go for the drive, the light and a beautiful nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' looks like a car trip and 'light' like brightness, but the drive is a compulsion and to light is to set fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyromania is an obsessive urge to start fires, that is, a compulsive drive to set things alight.

clue.text: Go over road for assignation

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written over another comes above it, so 'go' sits on top of 'road'

blocks.note: to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: Crossing the street to meet a lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go over' reads as one phrasal verb meaning cross or review; split it, and 'over' just places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is a secret romantic meeting arranged in advance, which is what an assignation is.

clue.text: Plastic casings removed from smaller cables

indicators.note: a casing is the outside layer, so each of the next two words loses its first and last letters

blocks.note: 'smaller' without its outer S and R
'cables' without its outer C and S

explanation.surface: An electrician stripping the plastic sheathing off thin cables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic' seems to be the casing material, but it is the definition, meaning easily shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: Plastic in its older sense means capable of being moulded or bent, exactly as malleable does.

clue.text: Comfort derived from phrasal verbs

indicators.note: the answer is drawn straight out of the letters of the words that follow

blocks.note: the tail of 'phrasal' plus the start of 'verbs'

explanation.surface: A grammar student taking solace in phrasal verbs.
explanation.walkthrough: SALVE as a noun is a soothing ointment, and figuratively anything that eases distress.
explanation.definitionFit: A salve soothes a wound or a troubled conscience, so it is a source of comfort or solace.

clue.text: Manager of St Johnstone, finally topping division

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the last letter of the name before it
in a down clue, whatever tops something comes above it, so the earlier pieces sit over 'division'

explanation.surface: Football news: the St Johnstone manager tops the league at last.
explanation.walkthrough: St Johnstone is a Scottish football club, so 'Manager of St Johnstone' reads as one phrase; the definition is 'Manager' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A steward is someone who runs an estate, household or event on another's behalf, a kind of manager.

clue.text: Fraction of distance from head to foot, top to toe

indicators.note: the letter at the top of a down entry moves to its toe, the bottom, shifting the rest up

explanation.surface: An anatomy lesson: the head is about one part in eight of a person's height.
explanation.walkthrough: Artists do reckon the head as one eighth of body height, so the surface is apt. Move HEIGHT's H from the top to the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: An eighth is one of eight equal parts, a specific fraction.

clue.text: Norwegian writer Nesbo is endlessly reviewed

indicators.note: each of the two words has its end cut off
to re-view is to look back, so the trimmed letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the crime novelist's name without its final O

explanation.surface: A books page panning the Norwegian thriller writer Jo Nesbo.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue offers one Norwegian writer, Nesbo, and defines another: Henrik Ibsen, the playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen, author of A Doll's House and Peer Gynt, is Norway's most celebrated dramatist.

clue.text: Label your bananas in colour

indicators.note: going bananas is going crazy, so the letters of 'label your' are scrambled

explanation.surface: An instruction to tag the fruit with a coloured sticker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the fruit being labelled, but it is slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal blue is a deep, vivid shade of blue, one specific colour.

clue.text: Female love is the ultimate in calm courage

indicators.note: the ultimate is the last, so only the final letter of 'calm' is kept

blocks.note: zero, as in a tennis score

explanation.surface: A claim that a woman's love is the supreme example of calm bravery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ultimate in calm courage' sounds like praise for the highest form of bravery; split it after 'calm'.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroism is great bravery shown in danger, a stronger synonym for courage.

clue.text: May ruffle feathers, losing face

indicators.note: the face of a word is its front, so the first letter of 'feathers' goes
ruffled feathers are disordered, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: 'feathers' with its first letter F dropped

explanation.surface: A political sketch: May upsets colleagues and is humiliated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May' opens the sentence, so its capital hides that it is a surname: Theresa May was UK Prime Minister from 2016 to 2019.
explanation.definitionFit: Theresa is the first name of former British Prime Minister May, so the surname clues the given name.

clue.text: State makes better shoe components

indicators.note: to state something is to say it out loud, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: to make better is to cure

explanation.surface: Someone claiming that good parts improve a shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a noun, a country or condition, but it is the verb, telling you to speak the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Heels are the raised back parts on the underside of shoes, one of the pieces a shoe is built from.

clue.text: Develop green site in national park

indicators.note: developing something changes its form, so the letters that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A planning row over building on a greenfield site inside a protected park.
explanation.walkthrough: A greenfield site is undeveloped land, so 'develop green site' reads as a property proposal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti in Tanzania is a famous protected wildlife reserve, one of Africa's best-known national parks.

clue.text: Spooner’s misfortunes necessitate a bloody complaint!

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words are exchanged

blocks.note: to necessitate is to need; it lends its N sound to the first half
setbacks, as in cruel blows; its BL sound moves to the second half

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry that bad luck calls for some bloody complaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' reads as a British swearword, and a complaint as a grumble; here it is literally bloody, and a complaint is an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosebleed is a minor ailment in which blood runs from the nostrils, a literally bloody medical complaint.

clue.text: Hispanic misses most mockery I’ve picked up

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter, so 'mockery' loses its tail
in a down clue, picking something up lifts it so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: satire is mockery, minus its last letter
'I've' means 'I have', and so does 'one's', as in one's done it

explanation.surface: Someone admitting they have absorbed the scorn aimed at Spanish women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' suggests hearing or learning, but in a down clue it lifts the pieces to read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Señoritas are young unmarried women in Spanish-speaking places, the equivalent of the English title miss.

clue.text: Puce latex, bafflingly free of charge

indicators.note: something baffling is confused, so the letters before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: An odd shopping find: purple-brown rubber given away for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free of charge' means gratis in the surface; here the charge is a criminal accusation and the phrase is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To exculpate someone is to clear them of blame, releasing them from an accusation.

clue.text: Sadly I want to arrest Queen Mum, part of underground network

indicators.note: things that go sadly go wrong, so the letters of 'I want' are rearranged
to arrest is to hold, so the rearranged letters hold the royal and parent pieces

explanation.surface: A plotter's regretful wish to detain the Queen Mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen Mum' reads as the late Queen Mother, but it is two pieces: ER then MA. 'Underground' is buried pipes, not the London Tube.
explanation.definitionFit: A water main is a large buried pipe carrying the public supply, one part of the underground distribution network.

clue.text: Amusing desire to eat a horse on the radio

indicators.note: whatever eats something takes it inside, so 'desire' swallows the other pieces
on the radio things are heard rather than seen, so the horse is written as it sounds

blocks.note: child's word for a horse, spelt as two letters

explanation.surface: A comic line: I'm so hungry I could eat a horse, spoken on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Gee-gee is a childish or racing word for a horse; only its sound is used, spelt as two letters. 'Eat a horse' is the idiom for great hunger.
explanation.definitionFit: Waggish means playfully humorous, like a wag or joker, so it is a synonym for amusing.

clue.text: Castilian hero regularly sells child

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every second letter of the following words is kept

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters of 'child', continuing the rhythm

explanation.surface: A scandal: a Spanish hero habitually trading in children.
explanation.walkthrough: El Cid was Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, the eleventh-century Castilian knight celebrated in Spain's national epic.
explanation.definitionFit: El Cid, the medieval Castilian warrior of legend and film, is Spain's great national champion.

clue.text: Thought of Rosa Klebb in action

indicators.note: the setter is placed inside the word for action

blocks.note: the setter's pseudonym refers to herself

explanation.surface: Musing on what the Bond villainess Rosa Klebb was like in action.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosa Klebb is the villain of From Russia with Love and also this puzzle's setter, so her name stands for the setter speaking of herself.
explanation.definitionFit: To deem is to judge or consider, so deemed is a past-tense synonym for thought, as in 'thought wise'.

clue.text: Grand lady surrounded by huge lizards

indicators.note: the lady is surrounded, so the word for huge goes around her

blocks.note: G is a grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: A grande dame hemmed in by enormous reptiles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand lady' reads as one phrase, a dowager; split it, 'Grand' being G.
explanation.definitionFit: Goannas are the large monitor lizards of Australia.

clue.text: Texting you after a long goodbye

indicators.note: the texting word for you is placed after the other pieces

blocks.note: to long for something is to be dying for it

explanation.surface: Someone signing off at length in a text message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A long goodbye' reads as a lengthy farewell; 'long' is the verb, to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is the French farewell, borrowed into English as a formal way to say goodbye.

clue.text: Leader of Lazio dons “squealed”, in common parlance

indicators.note: the leader is the front, so only the first letter of 'Lazio' is kept
to don is to put on clothing, so the first piece wears the word for 'squealed' around it

blocks.note: to sing is to inform to the police

explanation.surface: An Italian football captain accusing Mafia dons of informing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like a noun, Mafia bosses; it is the verb, puts on. Lazio is a Rome football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang is informal, everyday vocabulary, the language of common parlance rather than formal speech.

clue.text: Recurrent failure starts to vitiate early determination

indicators.note: recurrent means running back, so the failure is read backwards
the starts of words are their first letters, so only the openings of the next two words are kept

explanation.surface: Repeated failures start to erode a person's determination early on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recurrent failure' reads as repeated failing; 'recurrent' is the reversal signal and the failure is a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolve as a noun is firmness of purpose, a synonym for determination.

clue.text: Letter asking YMCA to exclude odd individuals

indicators.note: individuals are single characters, so every odd-numbered letter is left out and the even ones remain

blocks.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of 'asking'

explanation.surface: A letter asking a youth hostel to turn away eccentrics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd individuals' sounds like weird people; it means the letters in odd positions.
explanation.definitionFit: Sigma is the eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, the one for S.

clue.text: Can time stop popular time traveller?

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so the first pieces are plugged into the word for popular

explanation.surface: A sci-fi question: can Time halt a well-loved time-travelling hero?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time traveller' reads as one phrase, suggesting Doctor Who; the definition is 'traveller' alone. The container splits the word for popular after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An itinerant is someone who moves from place to place, a wanderer or traveller.

clue.text: Skin shows signs of ageing, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the word is spelt differently from how it is said

blocks.note: grey hairs appear as people age

explanation.surface: Wrinkled skin betrays the years, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skin' looks like a noun, the body's covering; it is a verb, to scrape the surface off.
explanation.definitionFit: To graze a knee is to scrape off some of its surface, which is to skin it.

clue.text: Reporting the way crime develops in residential areas

indicators.note: a report is spoken aloud, so the phrase that follows is judged by its sound

blocks.note: the way is how, crime is sin, develops is gestates

explanation.surface: A journalist covering how crime grows on council estates.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's report on crime is the homophone signal. A housing estate is a British planned development of homes, often council-built.
explanation.definitionFit: Housing estates are planned groups of homes built together, neighbourhoods designed for people to live in.
